lessons.title: Nouns — naming things
lessons.goal: Place the card TISCH on the sentence bar and put a chip on the Nominativ form.
explanation: Nouns name things, people and places: «Tisch» (table), «Frau» (woman), «Schule» (school). In German, nouns are ALWAYS capitalized — even in the middle of a sentence.
Every German noun has a grammatical gender: «der» (masculine), «die» (feminine) or «das» (neuter). You can see the gender in the colored banner on the card: blue = der, red = die, green = das.
The article changes depending on the noun's job in the sentence — these are the four CASES. When the noun is the subject (the doer), it uses the Nominativ: «der Tisch».
Try it: put the TISCH card on the bar and place a chip on the Nominativ form «der Tisch».

lessons.title: Verbs — action words
lessons.goal: Place the card SEIN on the bar and put a chip on the ich-form «bin».
explanation: Verbs describe actions and states: «gehen» (to go), «essen» (to eat), «sein» (to be). The form on the card's banner is the infinitive — the dictionary form.
In a real sentence the verb changes its ending to match the person: «ich bin» (I am), «du bist» (you are), «er/sie/es ist» (he/she/it is). This is called conjugation.
The six person chips are printed right on the verb card: ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie. Placing a chip picks the conjugated form.
Try it: place the verb SEIN and put the chip on the ich-form — «bin».

lessons.title: Pronouns — word doubles
lessons.goal: Place the pronoun card DU on the sentence bar.
explanation: Pronouns replace nouns: instead of «der Tisch» you can say «er» (it), instead of «die Frau» — «sie» (she). That is why the ER/SIE/ES card can stand in for any noun card.
The personal pronouns are: «ich» (I), «du» (you), «er/sie/es» (he/she/it), «wir» (we), «ihr» (you all), «sie» (they).
The pronoun decides which verb form you need — the chip on the verb must match the pronoun: «du» always pairs with the du-form, e.g. «du kommst».
Try it: place the DU card on the bar.

lessons.title: Your first sentence: subject + verb
lessons.goal: Build the sentence «Ich komme.» — and don't forget the chip on the verb!
explanation: Every German sentence needs a SUBJECT (who?) and a VERB (what happens?). The verb always sits in second position.
«Ich komme.» means «I come / I am coming.» The pronoun «ich» is the subject, so the verb «kommen» needs the ich-form «komme».
Place the ICH card, then the verb KOMMEN — and put the person chip on the ich-form. The chip proves you picked the right conjugation!

lessons.title: Subject + verb + object: the cases
lessons.goal: Build «Der Mann isst den Apfel.» — with the correct case chip on each noun.
explanation: Now we add an OBJECT: who eats? — «der Mann» (subject). What does he eat? — «den Apfel» (object).
This is where the German cases come in: the SUBJECT takes the Nominativ («der Mann»), the OBJECT takes the Akkusativ («den Apfel»). Watch how «der» changes to «den»!
You show the case by placing a chip on the noun card: Nominativ chip on MANN, Akkusativ chip on APFEL. The verb «essen» (to eat) needs the er-form «isst» to match «der Mann».
Build it: MANN + ESSEN + APFEL, chips on Nominativ, «isst», Akkusativ.

lessons.title: Asking questions
explanation: Question words (Fragewörter) like «wie» (how), «wer» (who), «woher» (where from) always open the sentence — and the verb comes second, right after them.
«Wie heißt du?» means «What is your name?» — literally «How are you called?». Note the word order: question word → verb → subject.
«du» is the subject, so «heißen» takes the du-form «heißt». Question cards carry a small explanation right on the card — use it!
Build it: WIE + HEISSEN (chip on «heißt») + DU.

lessons.title: Prepositions — little words, big cases
explanation: Prepositions connect places and people: «aus» (from), «mit» (with), «in» (in/into). The picture on each preposition card shows its meaning.
Important: the noun AFTER a preposition changes its case! «aus» and «mit» always take the Dativ: «aus der Schule», «mit dem Freund».
In «Ich komme aus der Schule.» (I come from school), «die Schule» follows «aus» — so put the Dativ chip on SCHULE. The verb chip is the ich-form «komme».
Build it: ICH + KOMMEN + AUS + SCHULE (Dativ chip!).

lessons.title: Two-way prepositions: movement or place?
lessons.goal: Build «Das Kind geht in die Schule.»
explanation: Prepositions like «in», «auf», «unter», «neben» are two-way (Wechselpräpositionen): with MOVEMENT (where to?) they take the Akkusativ, with POSITION (where?) the Dativ.
«Das Kind geht in die Schule.» (The child goes to school) — «gehen» is movement, so «die Schule» takes the Akkusativ: «in die Schule». (With position it would be «in der Schule» — Dativ.)
The subject «das Kind» needs the Nominativ chip, and «gehen» takes the er-form «geht».
Build it: KIND + GEHEN + IN + SCHULE — chips: Nominativ, «geht», Akkusativ.
lessons.targetSentence: Das Kind geht in die Schule.

lessons.title: Adjectives — describing things
explanation: Adjectives describe nouns: «hoch» (tall/high), «groß» (big), «klein» (small), «schön» (beautiful).
After the verb «sein» (to be), the adjective simply follows: «Der Tisch ist hoch.» (The table is tall.) No ending needed in this position!
The subject «der Tisch» still needs its Nominativ chip, and «sein» takes the er-form «ist».
Build it: TISCH + SEIN + HOCH — chips: Nominativ and «ist».

lessons.title: Modal verbs — wanting, musting, canning
lessons.goal: Build «Ich will spielen.» — modal verb + infinitive at the end!
explanation: Modal verbs express wishes and obligations: «wollen» (want), «müssen» (must), «können» (can). They are special cards: they NEVER play alone.
A modal verb always needs a partner: the main verb goes to the very END of the sentence in its infinitive form: «Ich will spielen.» (I want to play.)
The person chip goes on the MODAL verb — it is the conjugated one: «ich will». The main verb «spielen» stays untouched.
Build it: ICH + WOLLEN (chip «will») + SPIELEN.
